new_statements.quote: The most important feature of Kisi's suprasegmental inventory is the use of tone to signal lexical and grammatical differences. [...] The tonal system of Kisi has two level and two contour tones; the latter are, in some cases, transparently derived from level tones. [...] Another suprasegmental feature found in Kisi is contrastive vowel length for all monophthongal vowels. Consonant gemination, on the other hand, appears only in a few morphologically restricted environments. [p. 17:] Left dislocation and stress are other devices used for focus.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kisi is a tone language (two level + two contour tones, marginal extra-high) with contrastive vowel length; the prosodic inventory contains no word stress and no statement of stress placement is made. 'Stress' is mentioned only as a phrase-level focus device. Independently, Samarin 1950 (p. 90, saved file) lists the phonemes as 'consonants, vowels, tones, and juncture features' with three register tonemes (p. 96) and never uses the word stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Childs notes Northern Kisi differs phonologically from the described Southern variety (phonemic /r/ in the north; different scope of the l→t dissimilation rule; heavier Mandingo admixture), p. 10.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (lexical on nouns, grammatical on verbs); the one 'stress' remark concerns focus marking at utterance level, not word stress. Both opened primary descriptions (Childs 1995, Samarin 1950) describe Liberian = Southern Kisi [kss, sout2778], not Northern Kissi proper; no opened source gives a first-hand prosodic description of the Northern (Guinea/Sierra Leone) variety.
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened primary descriptions (Childs 1995; Samarin 1950) describe the Liberian = Southern Kisi variety, Glottolog sout2778 [kss]; Glottolog attaches Samarin 1950 to both kqs and kss. Northern Kissi (kisiduei; Guinea Kissidougou/Guéckédou and Sierra Leone Kailahun; Ethnologue dialects Liaro, Kama, Teng, Tung) is explicitly a distinct, phonologically different dialect per Childs 1995: 9-10, and no opened source gives a first-hand prosodic description of it. The only kqs-specific file opened (Tamba 2023, Sierra Leone) is silent on stress and tone.

sources.note: p. 90: 'The phonemes of Kisi consist of consonants, vowels, tones, and juncture features.' p. 96 §1c The Pitch Phonemes (Tonemes): 'There are three register tonemes in Kisi' (low, high, unmarked mid) with minimal pairs; §1d Juncture. The word 'stress' does not occur (count 0); 'accent' once, in the dialect sense (p. 89). Informant Moses Davis from Kpukulo/Sardu, western Liberia = Southern Kisi [kss].
